reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that NFL coaches suffer from recency bias and small-sample fallacy, leading them to overcorrect after a single pass play by increasing run frequency. This creates a predictable deviation from game-theoretic randomness. The mathematical structure is a sequential stochastic process where the next play type depends on the previous one, violating independence. The deviation manifests as a positive correlation between pass and subsequent run attempts, quantified by a ~25% increase in run likelihood. This can be modeled as a Markov chain with transition probabilities that deviate from uniformity. The second-order effect occurs on 2nd & long, where the rush spike is most pronounced (~44%), suggesting a strong psychological trigger. The failure mode arises when coaches misinterpret variance as a signal for imbalance, leading to predictable overcorrection. The epistemic risk lies in assuming that past outcomes influence future ones beyond what is statistically justified. The dual nature of this bias—both behavioral and statistical—means that while it appears random, it is actually deterministic within a bounded set of cognitive errors. The root cause is the misapplication of Bayesian updating in small samples, where prior beliefs dominate posterior estimates. This leads to a systematic overestimation of the probability of the opposite play type, creating exploitable edges in prop bets and game predictions.
